run.userPrompt:
A consumer goods company sells almost entirely through third-party retailers, who control shelf placement and customer data. Management wants a direct-to-consumer channel to capture first-party data and higher margins, but its two largest retail partners together account for 55% of revenue and have punished suppliers who competed with them directly. An earlier quiet pilot of a web store triggered an angry call from one partner's buying team.

Design a go-to-market plan for building a meaningful direct-to-consumer business while keeping the retail relationships that fund the company today. Specify the channel architecture, product and pricing differentiation between channels, the data strategy, and the partner-communication plan that prevents open channel conflict.

agentResponses.content:
**Go-to-Market Plan: The “Emissary” DTC Model** The objective is not to build a volume competitor to your retailers. It is to build a strategically *meaningful* direct channel—one that captures first-party data, yields higher margins on differentiated products, and strengthens the brand equity that drives retail sales—while offering your largest retail partners ironclad proof that you are not disintermediating them. The following plan treats DTC not as a sales outlet, but as a **customer-insight engine and brand experience layer** that operates under strict guardrails. --- ### 1. Strategic Doctrine: “Complement, Never Cannibalize” Your retailers control shelf placement and have a history of retaliation. Any DTC strategy that looks like a land grab will trigger a delisting threat. Establish these non-negotiable principles upfront and publish them internally and externally: * **Volume Ceiling.** Publicly commit (and contractually bind the DTC P&L) that direct sales will not exceed **8–10% of total company revenue** for the first three years. This signals to retail buyers that you are not chasing their volume. * **Assortment Firewall.** DTC will not carry the “hero” or top-volume SKUs that define the retail partnership. The direct channel sells what retail *cannot* economically carry: customization, limited editions, and bundled services. * **Price Parity.** DTC will never undercut retail’s everyday shelf price on comparable items. DTC value is delivered through exclusivity, service, and loyalty—not discounting. * **Data Reciprocity.** DTC insights will be shared back with retail partners to improve their assortment and sell-through, positioning your channel as a forecast lab, not a competitor. --- ### 2. Channel Architecture: The Three-Lattice System Do not launch a single “web store” that mirrors Amazon. Build a lattice of touchpoints, each with a distinct role. #### A. The Digital Flagship (DTC.com) *Role: High-margin incubator and zero-party data collection.* * **Curated, Non-Core Assortment Only.** Launch with three categories: (1) *Customization* (e.g., build-your-own bundles, monogramming, exclusive colors/sizes); (2) *Subscription/Replenishment* (if applicable, for consumables or refills); (3) *Limited Drops* (collaborations, seasonal micro-collections). * **No Search Arbitrage.** Do not buy Google Shopping ads on hero SKU terms that direct traffic away from retail. Instead, bid on brand + “custom,” “subscription,” or “official store” terms. * **“Find It Near You.”** For every core SKU, the product page on DTC.com displays a “Buy at Our Retail Partners” widget with local inventory lookup, driving foot traffic *to* them. #### B. The Retail-Integrated Layer (“Endless Aisle”) *Role: Prove DTC saves retail sales, not steals them.* * Offer your top two retail partners a pilot program: when their store is out of stock of a core SKU, their website or in-store kiosk routes the order to your DTC fulfillment engine. * **The partner keeps the sale revenue** (you fulfill at wholesale cost or take a pre-agreed logistics fee). This teaches the buying team to view your logistics capability as a safety net, not a rival. #### C. The Data Capture Layer (Mobile + Packaging) *Role: Turn every retail sale into a data relationship owned by the brand.* * **QR-First Packaging.** Every unit ships with a QR code leading to a 90-second registration flow: warranty activation, how-to content, and a “profile quiz” (skin type, household size, usage habits). Incentivize with a small gift (free sample, extended warranty) rather than a price discount. * **The Companion App.** Not a store, but a “membership hub.” Users track orders, access exclusive content, and manage subscriptions. Purchases happen in-app only for DTC-exclusives; core products deep-link to retail partner carts. --- ### 3. Product & Pricing Differentiation: The Firewall Framework Channel conflict ignites when customers can compare identical SKUs side-by-side. Remove comparability. | Dimension | Retail Channel | DTC Channel | |-----------|----------------|-------------| | **Core Assortment** | Hero SKUs, standard sizes, mass-market variants. | Not carried. | | **Exclusive Assortment** | None. | Custom builds, limited editions, oversized/refill formats, collaboration products. | | **New Launches** | 90-day retail-first window. | Early access for loyalty members only (limited units, not full rollout). | | **Pricing** | Promotional calendar; competitive shelf price. | MSRP parity on any comparable bundle. Value delivered via bundling, subscription savings, or loyalty points—never list-price undercutting. | | **Service** | Standard returns via retailer. | White-glove support, free customization, “pause or cancel anytime” subscription management. | **Example:** If your retail hero is a 12-oz lavender shampoo at $14.99, DTC never sells that exact item. DTC sells a “ scalp-profile quiz-matched” 16-oz refill pouch in a seasonal scent, bundled with a travel kit for $38. The per-ounce cost is comparable or higher; the product is incomparable. --- ### 4. Data Strategy: From Zero-Party to Network Intelligence Because retailers gate customer data, DTC must become a magnet for *voluntarily given* data, then use it to benefit the entire ecosystem. * **Zero-Party Data via Product Experience.** The QR registration and quiz yield psychographic profiles (preferences, routines, values) that scan data cannot provide. This is your proprietary moat. * **First-Party Transactional Data.** DTC captures full-basket economics, cross-sell patterns, and true customer lifetime value. Use this to identify high-LTV personas (e.g., “the subscription bundle buyer”) and inform retail pack-size recommendations. * **The Retail Halo.** Run geo-holdout tests: measure brick-and-mortar sell-through in markets with DTC brand advertising vs. control markets. Document the retail sales lift attributable to DTC awareness spend. Present this quarterly to buying teams as proof of incrementality. * **Data Reciprocity (The “Insight Report”).** Every quarter, share aggregated, anonymized DTC trends with retail partners: “DTC demand for unscented variants is up 40%; consider expanding your planogram.” This reframes your DTC database as a *category intelligence service* they receive for free. --- ### 5. Partner Communication Plan: The Transparency Protocol The failed pilot taught you that silence is interpreted as hostility. This time, lead with radical transparency. #### Before Launch: The Retail Partner Charter Draft a one-page public commitment letter signed by the CEO and shared with the top 10 retail partners. It should contain: 1. **The 8–10% Volume Cap** (auditable). 2. **The Assortment Firewall** (list of SKUs permanently excluded from DTC). 3. **Price Parity Enforcement** (adherence to unilateral MAP policies). 4. **Endless Aisle Offer** (formal proposal to fulfill their stock-outs). 5. **Data Sharing Schedule** (quarterly insight reports). #### The Narrative Reframe Do not say: *“We are launching DTC to capture margin.”* Say: *“We are launching a direct brand experience to recruit high-loyalty enthusiasts. Our data shows these enthusiasts spend 3x more annually across *all* channels, including your stores. We want to grow the pie, not steal the slice.”* #### The Quarterly Ecosystem Review Invite the buying teams from your top two partners to a formal quarterly business review that includes: * DTC customer demographics (show minimal overlap with their typical shopper). * DTC marketing spend and resulting branded search lift (Google Trends data showing increased demand at retail). * Endless aisle pilot results (units saved from stock-out attrition). * Co-development opportunities (e.g., “You get exclusive launch rights on the DTC bestseller we validated last quarter”). #### The Escalation Brake Give each top partner a designated “channel integrity” liaison with direct access to your Chief Commercial Officer. If they perceive encroachment, they have a 48-hour escalation path to resolve before it becomes a public conflict. --- ### 6. Implementation Roadmap: A 15-Month Sequence | Phase | Timeline | Actions | |-------|----------|---------| | **Phase 1: Foundation** | Months 0–3 | • Freeze the hero-SKU exclusion list.
• Redesign packaging with QR registration flow; launch loyalty hub (no store yet).
• Draft and circulate the Retail Partner Charter.
• Hire a DTC GM with P&L autonomy and a mandate *not* to compete with the national accounts team. | | **Phase 2: Soft Launch** | Months 4–9 | • Launch DTC.com with **only** customization and limited drops (no core SKUs).
• Approach one friendly retail partner with the Endless Aisle pilot.
• Run first geo-holdout test to measure retail halo.
• Share first quarterly insight report with partners. | | **Phase 3: Proof Point** | Months 10–15 | • Add subscription/replenishment if applicable.
• Expand Endless Aisle to second retail partner.
• Publish internal case study showing DTC-driven retail lift.
• Host first joint “Ecosystem Review” with top partners, presenting DTC as a forecast tool. | | **Phase 4: Controlled Scale** | Month 15+ | • If data proves incrementality, cautiously test one or two “retail-exhaust” SKUs (slow-moving sizes) DTC-only.
• Maintain the 10% revenue cap. Evaluate lifting it only after 24 months of partner trust. | --- ### 7. Governance & Internal Safeguards * **Separate P&L and Compensation.** The DTC team must not be paid on gross revenue if it incentivizes volume over guidelines. Compensate them on **data yield** (profiles captured), **DTC gross margin**, and **retail sell-through in their markets** (to align incentives). * **The “Red Team.”** Assign a member of the national accounts team to formally challenge every DTC promotion and SKU addition. If it violates the Charter, it does not ship. * **Executive Air Cover.** The CEO or COO must personally own the retail partner conversations. A DTC launch led by the digital team looks tactical; led by the C-suite, it looks strategic. --- ### Bottom Line Build a DTC business that is **meaningful in data and margin, but modest in volume.** Sell what retail cannot sell, price at or above retail parity, and use the channel to recruit enthusiasts whose behavior you can measure and share back. By offering your largest partners an Endless Aisle safety net, quarterly data dividends, and a public volume ceiling, you convert their suspicion into guarded partnership. The goal is not to outgrow your retailers; it is to know your end consumer better *through* them—and in spite of them.
